analysis.body:
# Interconnection Queue Snapshot: September 2026

The five major US grid operators are sitting on approximately 1.33 million megawatts of generation and storage projects awaiting connection, spread across 8,377 formal requests. ERCOT's Texas queue dominates at 438,000 MW, followed by NYISO's 319,000 MW, MISO's 300,000 MW, SPP's 198,000 MW, and CAISO's 72,000 MW. These queues reflect plans that have cleared initial screening but range from early study phases to near-commissioning, so they do not represent near-term buildout. Storage projects total roughly 327,000 MW across all five operators, while gas capacity sits at 184,000 MW—both categories tend to grow when data center load anchors new generation, even though the queues themselves measure grid-operator requests, not data center demand directly.

Commercial electricity sales in key data-center states tell a different story. Texas leads at 15,754 MWh in June 2026, followed by California at 10,025 MWh, but California's commercial rate is three times higher at $27.33 per MWh versus Texas at $8.66, reflecting both scarcity and policy. Virginia, Georgia, Ohio, and Arizona combined consumed 22,888 MWh at mid-range rates between $10.99 and $14.53, with Arizona and Oregon offering cheaper alternatives at $12.47 and $10.59 respectively. This pricing dispersion will likely drive siting decisions, since the queue pipeline ensures generation capacity is being planned across all regions, but cost remains a differentiator for load-intensive operations.

The composition of queued capacity reveals what infrastructure operators expect to support. Solar dominates by megawatts at roughly 279,000 MW across operators, wind adds 170,000 MW, and the combined 327,000 MW of storage suggests grids are explicitly planning for intermittency management—a structural shift driven partly by large, flat-load tenants like data centers requiring reliable supply. Watch next for which of these queued projects actually enter service and at what pace, since the gap between planned and commissioned capacity will indicate whether grids can absorb accelerating demand or face prolonged constraints.
